extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of advertising history; historians and scholars of 18th-century print culture; practitioners interested in historical advertising practices
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and standards for composing and judging mid‑18th‑century newspaper advertisements (stylistic, ethical, procedural and informational norms), illustrated with historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination to the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Every art ought to be exercised in due subordination to the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers should consider social responsibility: avoid practices that harm public interest or manipulate civic life. Example criticism: lottery registrars inviting customers by recounting last year's prizes is questioned as playing wantonly with public passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid playing wantonly with the public's passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether advertisers 'play too wantonly with our passions' (e.g., inflaming hopes or fears to sell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exploit strong emotions gratuitously to sell goods; avoid sensational or emotionally manipulative copy. The text cites the lottery registrar and heated advertising controversies (asperity of language) as undesirable examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit self‑praise but not censure of rivals
rubrics_metrics.description: In an advertisement it is allowed to every man to speak well of himself, but ... he should not assume the privilege of censuring his neighbour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote one's own product or skill but avoid attacking or excluding competitors on advertising copy—self‑promotion is acceptable, libelous or censorious statements are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertise with consciousness of public character and association
rubrics_metrics.description: The advertiser should remember that his name will stand in the same paper with those of great personages, and endeavour to make himself worthy of such association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with decorum and regard for reputation; consider how appearance beside high‑status notices will reflect on you and on posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay regard to posterity / durability of statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some regard is likewise to be paid to posterity; papers are saved and read in later ages, creating lasting records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid transient, contradictory, or false claims that will mislead future readers; craft durable, accurate statements because advertisements may be preserved and read by future generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improper disposition/association of advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: The noblest objects may be so associated as to be made ridiculous by adjacent trivial ads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of layout/context: placing a dignified notice next to a trivial or ludicrous ad can diminish perceived dignity (example: sublime natural history items juxtaposed with Daffy's Elixir or Dublin butter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'puffing' and disguised/lying advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of 'puffing' (insincere/flattered notices) and 'lying paragraphs' that are really advertisements in disguise is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert paid or deceptive 'puffs' posing as independent praise; reviewers and editors should mark and resist grosser instances (example: the 'Minister of State' puff eliciting reviewer wrath).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish surreptitious or dummy advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers complained of 'dummy' or gratuitous advertisements inserted to draw attention to other notices; unauthorized publications can mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish only accurate, authorized ads; theatrical managers forbade other papers from publishing their plays without authority because surreptitious notices led to errors and misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misrepresentation and gross errors in classified/subject headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Other publishers may commit 'gross Errors, as mentioning one Play for another, falsely representing the Parts, etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure accuracy in titles, parts, and subject matter; avoid false representation of the advertised event/product to prevent public misinfo and detriment to reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about transactional details (price, place, seller, instructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements should give clear transactional information: where sold, price, who sells, and any customer instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete purchasing details (seller's name & address, price, special instructions such as 'Ladies sending their servants are humbly desired to send a Glove of the size'). Example: Warren & Co. glove ad gives price, address, and ordering instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide specific identifying details in fugitive/reward notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Fugitive/deserter notices list age, height, posture, clothing, birthplace, trade, date of absence, and reward amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sufficiently precise physical and circumstantial descriptions and reward/claim instructions so apprehension or identification is practicable (example: William Beven deserter notice with height, clothes, birth parish, and 20 shillings reward).

rubrics_metrics.name: Official notices should state procedural/documentary requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Official communications must give formal instructions and required documentation (e.g., where medals will be delivered and that persons sent must bring cards signed and sealed with arms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issuing legal/official notices, state exact procedures, times, and documentary requirements to allow proper compliance (example: delivery of coronation medals requires signed/sealed cards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Event notices must supply program, schedule, venue and ticketing information
rubrics_metrics.description: Charity/feast announcements list sermon time, dinner time, performers, ticket price, where to obtain tickets, and special arrangements (e.g., two ladies' tickets for church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full logistical and program details so attendees know schedule, entertainment, costs, and ticket points of sale (example: Magdalen House Charity notice giving sermon time, dinner time, music details, ticket price and outlets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport/service ads should state schedule, fares and baggage rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Carriage/coach notices specify departure days/times, fares for different passenger types, and baggage/valuables policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about timetables, pricing and what is or isn't carried (example: Reading Machine advertises departure days, 6s fare, children in lap, and that it 'takes no charge of Writings, Money, Watches, or Jewels, unless entered').

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward extravagant medicinal claims / avoid quackery
rubrics_metrics.description: The text criticises quacks and extravagant promises (cosmetics and remedies claiming permanent effects or cures for many ailments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical and cosmetic advertisements should avoid implausible, blanket cure claims and be cautious about asserting permanent or universal effects; the author flags many such claims as suspect (examples: Warham's Balsam and other 'sovereign' remedies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state special conditions and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of explicit notices (N.B., P.S., limitation clauses) to make practical restrictions clear (e.g., minimum purchase sizes, sealing requirements, secrecy assurances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make special terms clear and prominent: minimum quantities ('No less a quantity ... than one Ounce'), secrecy assurances for sensitive adverts, or special return/collection conditions.
